rationale: Both are real-world cohort studies of durvalumab consolidation after chemoradiotherapy in unresectable stage III NSCLC, evaluating the same intervention/comparator/outcome pairing (durvalumab consolidation vs none, PFS and OS). Stuschke's CRISP-registry cohort reports a significant PFS benefit and a favorable-but-not-statistically-significant OS trend across its whole durvalumab-treated population. Selke's single-center cohort, stratified by PD-L1 status, shows that benefit is not uniform: durvalumab significantly improved both OS and PFS specifically in PD-L1-positive patients (p=0.043, p=0.027), while PD-L1-negative patients showed no significant survival difference. Selke's subgroup finding qualifies Stuschke's whole-population result by identifying PD-L1 status as a likely driver of who benefits.

rationale: Dang's meta-analysis pools 28 randomized controlled trials (14,758 patients) and finds PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors combined with chemotherapy improve overall survival versus chemotherapy alone in first-line advanced NSCLC. Katsarolis's independent real-world Greek cohort (610 patients eligible for outcome analysis) finds the same directional result outside the trial setting: immunotherapy at any line of treatment was associated with substantially longer OS than chemotherapy alone (17.5 vs 8.6 months; HR 0.51). An independent, non-overlapping real-world data source corroborating a pooled-RCT finding is direct support, not a restatement of the same data.

rationale: Dang's meta-analysis reports that PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors plus chemotherapy improve OS versus chemotherapy alone across the pooled first-line advanced NSCLC population. Liao's biomarker-stratified analysis of the phase 3 ORIENT-11 trial (a PD-1-inhibitor-plus-chemotherapy-vs-chemotherapy-alone trial, the same comparator structure as Dang's pooled evidence) shows this benefit is not uniform across all patients: high-ICPscore patients had a large PFS/OS benefit (HR 0.15/0.32), while low-ICPscore patients showed no significant benefit on either endpoint (HR 0.90/1.31). Liao's finding qualifies Dang's aggregate result by identifying a genomic biomarker subgroup in which the pooled-population benefit does not hold.

rationale: Dang's meta-analysis establishes that PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors plus chemotherapy improve OS versus chemotherapy alone across the general first-line advanced, driver-mutation-negative NSCLC population. Wu's Bayesian network meta-analysis restricts the same comparison (PD-1 inhibitor plus chemotherapy vs chemotherapy alone) to a specific, harder-to-treat subgroup -- driver-gene-negative NSCLC patients with liver metastases -- and finds the same directional PFS/OS benefit holds there too (HR 0.572/0.681). This extends Dang's broader-population finding into a clinically important, prognostically worse subgroup rather than retesting the same population, so it contextualizes rather than merely supports or qualifies.

rationale: Nodbrant's Swedish registry study finds that lung cancer patients on palliative immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment with a good baseline ECOG performance status (0-1) have substantially longer median OS than those with worse baseline status (PS 2 or 3). Machado's independent real-world meta-analysis of 12 studies (17,506 patients) receiving first-line pembrolizumab specifically finds the same directional predictor: ECOG status >=2 was associated with worse OS (HR 2.05). Two independent real-world evidence sources -- one a single-country registry across ICI regimens, one a pooled multi-study meta-analysis specific to pembrolizumab -- reach the same conclusion about performance status predicting checkpoint-inhibitor outcomes.
